Supportive Token Revealing for Fast Diffusion Language Model Decoding

Giries Abu Ayoub Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Haifa    Mario Barbara Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Haifa    Lluís Pastor-Pérez Affiliation: Institute for AI, University of Stuttgart    Tanja Bien Affiliation: Institute for AI, University of Stuttgart    Aneesh Barthakur Affiliation: Institute for AI, University of Stuttgart    Alaa Maalouf Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Haifa    Loay Mualem ††thanks: Corresponding author Affiliation: Institute for AI, University of Stuttgart Affiliation: IMPRS-IS Please send any questions to: jerryabuayob@gmail.com
Abstract

Discrete diffusion language models can generate text efficiently by updating multiple masked positions in parallel, but this parallelism introduces a quality-latency trade-off. Aggressive decoding may commit mutually dependent tokens too early, while conservative decoding requires many denoising steps. Existing methods address this tension by deciding which tokens are safe to reveal using confidence or dependency criteria. However, avoiding unsafe commits does not necessarily make the remaining masked sequence easy to decode, since uncertain tokens may depend on masked tokens, creating a bottleneck for denoising steps. We propose AXON, a training-free module that can be added on top of existing parallel decoding strategies for diffusion language models. Rather than replacing the base decoder, AXON monitors the remaining uncertain masked tokens and intervenes only when their current state suggests that additional context is needed. It then shifts the criterion from which tokens are safest to reveal to which confident reveals would best support later denoising. AXON selects anchors, confident masked tokens that uncertain positions attend to, using attention, uncertainty, and confidence signals. Experiments on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks across multiple diffusion language models show that AXON improves the quality-latency trade-off of existing parallel decoders, often reducing the number of function evaluations while maintaining or improving accuracy.

1 Introduction

Autoregressive language models radford2019ar1; brown2020ar2 generate text one token at a time, which makes their inference inherently sequential. Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) shi2024simplified; sahoo2024dllm1; li2022dlmm2; gong2022dlmm3; louddiscretedlmm4 offer a different generation paradigm: they start from a masked sequence and iteratively denoise it, predicting all masked positions at each step. This bidirectional refinement process makes dLLMs attractive for low-latency text generation since multiple positions can be updated in parallel. Recent dLLMs such as LLaDA nie2026llada and Dream ye2025dream demonstrate that this paradigm can produce competitive text generations while exposing a natural source of parallelism that is absent in autoregresive left-to-right decoding. However, unmasking arbitrary tokens simultaneously can produce inconsistent configurations as tokens may be coupled through syntax, semantics, arithmetic constraints, or multi-token entities. Existing training-free parallel-decoding methods mainly address this issue by deciding which tokens can be safely committed together. Confidence-based methods wu2025fastdllm; ben2026ebsampler; kim2026klass; shu2026dcd reveal tokens whose marginal probabilities are sufficiently high, implicitly assuming that high confidence tokens are both reliable and uncoupled/mutually independent. More recent dependency-aware methods luo2026dawn; ringel2026dependency; zhou2026attention; kim2026dependency use attention or distributional similarity to estimate interactions between masked positions and to avoid simultaneously committing strongly coupled tokens. However, even when unsafe commits are avoided, the remaining masked positions may still lack sufficient visible context for reliable parallel decoding. This creates a bottleneck where decoding becomes increasingly conservative or stalls altogether.

In this work, we take a complementary view of fast dLLM decoding. Instead of only asking which tokens are safe to reveal immediately, we ask which masked tokens would provide the most useful context for the remaining uncertain positions if revealed early. Some tokens are already easy to commit because they are confident and weakly coupled to others. Other tokens are influential because many uncertain positions attend to them or depend on them. Revealing such tokens can improve contextual support for later denoising steps and reduce decoding bottlenecks.

Motivated by this view, we propose AXON** * We call our method AXON by analogy to axons in neural systems: it reveals a few high-impact tokens that transmit useful context to uncertain positions during denoising., a training-free module that can be added on top of existing parallel decoding strategies. AXON treats influential-token revealing as a small set-selection problem. It scores candidate tokens using attention, uncertainty, and confidence signals, and selects a small non-redundant subset through a coverage-based objective. The coverage view naturally leads to a submodular function objective, since once an uncertain position is already supported by one selected token (i.e. covered), another token supporting the same position should contribute less additional value. Since this selection is not needed at every step, AXON uses a lightweight gate that activates it only when the current masked tokens appears under-supported. Figure 1 provides an overview of this process.

We evaluate AXON on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks across multiple diffusion language models and parallel decoders. The results show that AXON improves the quality-latency trade-off over strong baselines. Explicitly, our contributions are as follows :

  • •

    We introduce a complementary view of fast dLLM decoding: beyond selecting tokens that are safe to commit, a decoder can reveal informative masked tokens that provide useful context for the remaining positions.

  • •

    We propose AXON, a training-free module for existing parallel dLLM decoders. AXON intervenes only when the current masked sequence appears under-supported. It first applies a gate to detect such states, then identifies confident masked tokens that are strongly attended to by uncertain positions, and finally selects a non-redundant subset of these anchors through a coverage-based objective. Revealing the selected anchors provides targeted context to the remaining masked positions without modifying the underlying model.

  • •

    We evaluate AXON across multiple backbones, reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, and several families of parallel decoders, including confidence-based, locality-aware, and dependency-aware strategies. Across these settings, AXON improves the quality-latency trade-off while keeping the backbone frozen.

2 Related Work

Fast dLLM inference methods primarily differ in how masked positions are selected and revealed during denoising. In the sequel, we first review discrete dLLMs, followed by training-free decoding methods for frozen backbones and dependency-aware parallel decoding methods.

Discrete dLLMs. Extending denoising diffusion to discrete spaces, discrete dLLMs parameterize the reverse process through per-token marginal predictions (shi2024simplified; hoogeboom2021argmax; austin2021structured; sahoo2024dllm1; muller2026support). Recent large-scale masked dLLMs like LLaDA (nie2026llada; bie2025llada2; bie2026llada2) and Dream (ye2025dream) offer a competitive alternative to autoregressive generation.

Fast decoding and commit expansion for frozen dLLMs. A way to accelerate decoding is to predict multiple tokens per model call. In autoregressive models, speculative decoding and related verification-based methods propose multiple future tokens and validate them in parallel with the target model (leviathan2023speculative). For dLLMs, the challenge is to decide which masked positions can be reliably committed together. Early approaches make this choice using local uncertainty measures such as entropy, margin, or confidence (ghazvininejad2019mask). Fast-dLLM (wu2025fastdllm) combines block-wise Key-Value caching with a rule that commits positions whose marginal confidence exceeds a threshold, using high confidence as a proxy for reliable parallel commitment. EB-Sampler (ben2026ebsampler) uses an entropy bound to adaptively choose which and how many tokens to unmask at each step. KLASS (kim2026klass) requires the token’s distribution to be both confident and stable across successive denoising steps. LocalLeap (kong2025localleap) expands commits around confident anchors by relaxing nearby positions within a local window when local predictions appear reliable. These methods are lightweight and training-free, and they provide different criteria for expanding or accepting commits in a frozen dLLM.

Dependency-aware parallel decoding. Recent work has shown that aggressive parallel decoding can suffer from joint inconsistency, where tokens that look plausible individually become incompatible when committed together (wu2025fastdllm; ben2026ebsampler; zhang2026generation). Dependency-aware methods address this by estimating interactions between masked positions during decoding. APD (israel2026adp) uses an auxiliary autoregressive model to estimate dependencies between tokens committed in parallel. Similarly, DEMASK (ringel2026dependency) uses a lightweight pairwise dependency predictor trained on hidden states. Instead of training a model, other methods utilize the already available attention maps to estimate dependencies. Attn-Sampler (zhou2026attention) uses attention column sums as a global importance score for ordering commits. DAPD (kim2026dependency) builds an attention-induced Markov random field and picks per-step commits as a greedy independent set. DAWN (luo2026dawn) constructs an attention dependency graph and uses committed anchors to support decoding of related positions, with conflict-aware scheduling that avoids jointly updating strongly coupled positions.

These methods highlight the role of dependency structure in safe parallel commitment, but they primarily use it to decide which positions should or should not be updated together. AXON instead focuses on the complementary problem of anchor selection: identifying confident reveals that are not only reliable, but also informative for the remaining uncertain positions. Additional related work can be found in Appendix A .

3 Background

Diffusion language models generate a sequence by gradually resolving masked positions. Let XX denote the prompt and let y=(y1,…,yL)y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{L}) denote the response to be generated, where each yiy_{i} belongs to a discrete vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Decoding starts from a fully masked response, y(0)=([MASK],…,[MASK]),y^{(0)}=(\texttt{[MASK]}{},\ldots,\texttt{[MASK]}{}), and proceeds through a sequence of denoising steps. At step tt, the current response y(t)y^{(t)} contains both revealed tokens and still-masked positions. We denote the set of masked positions by M(t)={i∈{1,…,L}:yi(t)=[MASK]}.M^{(t)}=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,L\}:y_{i}^{(t)}=\texttt{[MASK]}{}\}. For every i∈M(t)i\in M^{(t)}, the model predicts a categorical distribution over the vocabulary, pθ​(yi=v∣X,y(t)),v∈𝒱,p_{\theta}(y_{i}=v\mid X,y^{(t)}),v\in\mathcal{V}, and we define its confidence as the probability assigned to the most likely non-mask token. A decoding rule then chooses a subset of masked positions R(t)⊆M(t)R^{(t)}\subseteq M^{(t)} to reveal. The selected positions are filled with their top-1 predictions and remain visible in the following denoising steps. Thus, the main inference-time decision is how to choose R(t)R^{(t)} at each step.

Parallel decoding. The advantage of dLLMs comes from the ability to reveal more than one position per forward pass. Revealing many positions reduces the number of denoising steps, but it can also introduce errors because the model gives per-position marginal predictions while the selected positions may be interdependent. A parallel decoder effectively relies on the approximation pθ​(yR∣X,y(t))≈∏i∈Rpθ​(yi∣X,y(t)),\;p_{\theta}(y_{R}\mid X,y^{(t)})\approx\prod_{i\in R}p_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid X,y^{(t)}), for the selected set RR. This approximation is reliable when the positions in RR are close to conditionally independent under the current context. In practice, masked tokens can depend on one another through syntax, semantics, arithmetic constraints, formatting, or multi-token entities. Thus, tokens that look plausible individually may form an inconsistent joint assignment when revealed together.

Notation. Let XX denotes the conditioning prompt. At a given step tt, let y(t)y^{(t)} the set of tokens already revealed, B(t)B^{(t)} denote the set of all token positions in the current decoding block, M(t)M^{(t)} be the set of positions that are still masked, and let U(t)⊆M(t)U^{(t)}\subseteq M^{(t)} be the set of (uncertain) positions whose predicted confidence falls below a threshold. Let Sbase(t)S^{(t)}_{\text{base}} denote the set of tokens that is proposed by the base decoder, and S⋆(t)S^{\star(t)} be the set of (final) tokens returned by AXON. We denote by ci(t)∈[0,1]c_{i}^{(t)}\in[0,1] the predicted confidence at position ii, by Ai​j(t)A_{ij}^{(t)} the attention weight that position ii assigns to position jj, aggregated across all attention layers. Finally α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] denotes the gate hyperparameter.

4 Methodology

Current fast parallel decoders may reveal several positions simultaneously if they are approximately conditionally independent. However, “safe” combinations don’t always provide enough context for future steps, leading to states where the remaining positions are still too uncertain to decode safely. AXON targets this limitation by augmenting a given decoder with a two stage strategy. First, AXON computes a lightweight condition to determine if the base decoder needs additional contextual support. Second, if the condition is satisfied (i.e. the gate activates), then AXON exposes one or more anchors—which are masked positions that are both confident, and receive strong attention from uncertain positions. By revealing these anchors, AXON exposes the necessary information required to reduce the uncertainty of the masked tokens. Figure 2 illustrates this process.

Anchors.

Ideally, an anchor should be a position that reduces the uncertainty of several masked positions once revealed. Given a masked position ii, the improvement of revealing position jj is ideally measured by the quantity Δi​(j)=H⁡(yi∣X,y(t))−H⁡(yi∣X,y(t),yj),\Delta_{i}(j)=H(y_{i}\mid X,y^{(t)})-H(y_{i}\mid X,y^{(t)},y_{j}), where HH denotes the entropy of the predictive distribution and yi,yjy_{i},y_{j} are the tokens at positions ii and jj. Optimizing Δi​(j)\Delta_{i}(j) directly is infeasible because the second term requires re-evaluating the model for each candidate anchor position.

Inspired by previous attention-based decoding methods luo2026dawn; zhou2026attention, we circumvent this limitation by using a lightweight score based on the attention maps of the dLLM which are already available as a by-product of the denoising step. Explicitly, define

wi​j(t)=Ai​j(t)​(1−ci(t))​cj(t),\displaystyle w_{ij}^{(t)}=A_{ij}^{(t)}\bigl(1-c_{i}^{(t)}\bigr)c_{j}^{(t)}, (1)

The confidence term cj(t)c_{j}^{(t)} selects for anchors that are confident and reliable, while the uncertainty term (1−ci(t))(1-c_{i}^{(t)}) emphasizes uncertain tokens that have the most need for additional context. Finally, the attention score Ai​j(t)A_{ij}^{(t)} captures the fact that the uncertainty for a masked position ii has the most potential for improvement when it is strongly coupled with the anchor jj. Indeed, the connection between attention and confidence improvement can be empirically verified (see Figure 7), further supported by the attention-dynamics and coverage analyses (see Appendix C), and made more rigorous for single-layer dLLMs (see Appendix G).

Coverage objective. The anchor score above measures the usefulness of one candidate anchor for one uncertain position. However, when selecting multiple anchors at a denoising step (see Section 5), their value should not be treated independently. Two anchors may both appear useful, but if they support the same uncertain positions, revealing both gives little additional benefit. We therefore select anchors by maximizing a coverage objective under a cardinality constraint:

maxS⊆V(t),|S|≤k⁡C(t)​(S)=∑i∈U(t)maxj∈S⁡wi​j(t),\max_{S\subseteq V^{(t)},\,|S|\leq k}C^{(t)}(S)=\sum_{i\in U^{(t)}}\max_{j\in S}w_{ij}^{(t)}, (2)

where SS is the selected anchor set, and kk is the anchor budget. Each uncertain position receives credit only from its best selected anchor, encouraging selected anchors to cover different parts of the residual state.

Proposition D in Appendix D proves that C⁡(S)C(S) (Eq. 2) is monotone submodular, giving diminishing returns when anchors cover overlapping uncertain positions. Formally, a set function CC is submodular if for every X⊆YX\subseteq Y and j∉Yj\notin Y,

C⁡(X∪{j})−C⁡(X)≥C⁡(Y∪{j})−C⁡(Y).C(X\cup\{j\})-C(X)\geq C(Y\cup\{j\})-C(Y).

Submodular functions enjoy the property that under a cardinality budget kk, simple greedy maximization gives a (1−1/e)(1-1/e) approximation guarantee (nemhauser1978analysis). Overall, C⁡(S)C(S) encourages early (greedy) anchors to target the largest pockets of uncertainty, leading to total support rising quickly and then saturating.

4.1 Gating mechanisms

To effectively augment different base decoders with AXON, we develop a mechanism to conditionally activate AXON (i.e. a gate) when the base decoder needs additional support. Our gate is computationally efficient as it depends solely on signals already computed during the forward pass. It detects two common failure modes of base decoders, namely (a) a “pace deficit”, and (b) a “context deficit”—which we detail in the immediate sequel.

Pace deficit criterion.

It is often desirable to enforce a fixed budget of diffusion steps, say T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N}. At time step tt there are |M(t)||M^{(t)}| tokens that still need to be revealed and only T−tT-t steps remaining. An estimate of the fraction of the remaining masked tokens that should be revealed at step tt to enforce this budget is, ρ(t)=1T−t\rho^{(t)}=\frac{1}{T-t}. We interpret ρ(t)\rho^{(t)} as the required pace. Analogously, the base decoder’s pace is simply the fraction of masked tokens revealed at step tt, i.e. r(t)=|Sbase(t)||M(t)|r^{(t)}=\frac{|S^{(t)}_{\text{base}}|}{|M^{(t)}|}. Thus, to detect a deficit in the pace, we compute the following quantity,

dpace(t)=(ρ(t)−r(t))𝕀[r(t)≤r(t−1)].d_{\text{pace}}^{(t)}=\big(\rho^{(t)}-r^{(t)}\big)\,\mathbb{I}\!\big[r^{(t)}\leq r^{(t-1)}\,\big]. (3)

Here 𝕀⁡[⋅]\mathbb{I}[\cdot] denotes an indicator function. The term ρ(t)−r(t)\rho^{(t)}-r^{(t)} is a straightforward realization of the pace deficit, while the condition r(t)≤r(t−1)r^{(t)}\leq r^{(t-1)} allows AXON to ignore the pace deficit when the base decoder’s pace is still increasing, i.e. AXON is optimistic that the pace deficit will be solved by the base decoder in subsequent steps.

Context deficit criterion. One of the core goals of AXON is to improve the contextual support provided by decoded tokens. Given the base decoder’s proposal, we can compute a normalized measure of the contextual support as follows,

g(t)=1|U(t)|​∑i∈U(t)∑j∈Sbase(t)Ai​j(t)∑j∈B(t)Ai​j(t)+ε.g^{(t)}=\frac{1}{|U^{(t)}|}\sum_{i\in U^{(t)}}\frac{\sum_{j\in S^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}}}A_{ij}^{(t)}}{\sum_{j\in B^{(t)}}A_{ij}^{(t)}+\varepsilon}. (4)

Each term in the outer sum measures the support (in terms of attention) provided by Sbase(t)S^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}} to position ii, relative to the total support provided by all the tokens in the block. To detect low contextual support, we compare g(t)g^{(t)} to a dynamic threshold to obtain our context deficit criterion, namely,

dctx(t)=max⁡(r(t),uM(t))−g(t),d_{\text{ctx}}^{(t)}=\max\!\big(r^{(t)},\,u_{M}^{(t)}\big)-g^{(t)}, (5)

where r(t)=|Sbase(t)||M(t)|r^{(t)}=\frac{|S^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}}|}{|M^{(t)}|} as before, and uM(t)=1|U(t)|​∑i∈U(t)(1−ci(t))u_{M}^{(t)}=\frac{1}{|U^{(t)}|}\sum_{i\in U^{(t)}}(1-c_{i}^{(t)}) is the mean uncertainty among uncertain tokens. The dynamic threshold captures two scenarios where we want to increase the contextual support further (by activating AXON). Firstly, when r(t)r^{(t)} is high, it means that the base decoder has committed a large number of positions, and so the contextual support should be proportionately high to avoid committing tokens that provide low support. Secondly, when uM(t)u_{M}^{(t)} is high, this means that the remaining masked tokens are highly uncertain, and so again, the contextual support should be increased proportionately. We refer the reader to Section K in the Appendix for an ablation and additional analysis of alternative scalings of these two terms. In particular, one can introduce separate weights or normalization factors for the reveal ratio and uncertainty terms. However, our experiments show that keeping both signals on their natural scale, i.e., using the unweighted form in Eq. (5), gives the best and most stable performance. This shows that the two quantities are already comparable enough for gating purposes.

Hybrid gate. We combine both gates into an α\alpha-weighted hybrid gate:

Gα(t)=𝕀[α(dctx(t))++(1−α)(dpace(t))+>0],G_{\alpha}^{(t)}\;=\;\mathbb{I}\!\Big[\,\alpha\,\big(d_{\text{ctx}}^{(t)}\big)_{+}+(1-\alpha)\,\big(d_{\text{pace}}^{(t)}\big)_{+}>0\,\Big], (6)

where (x)+=max⁡(0,x)(x)_{+}=\max(0,x) ensures that a negative deficit (surplus) in one criterion does not offset the other. When the gate is activated, AXON’s anchor selection procedure kicks into action; otherwise, AXON commits the base proposal. The effect of changing α\alpha, which modulates the emphasis on the pace deficit and context criteria, is studied in Appendix  F. Activation patterns for Gα(t)G_{\alpha}^{(t)} as a function of tt is visualized in Figure 3. For additional analysis on gate firing patterns see Appendix I.

5 Experiments

We evaluate our framework against standard discrete diffusion benchmarks. We focus on 3 metrics: the quality-latency trade-off and the number of computational steps of our dynamic mechanism.

5.1 Setups

Models and datasets. We evaluate AXON on three dLLM backbones spanning two model families: Dream-v0-Instruct-7B†† † https://huggingface.co/Dream-org/Dream-v0-Instruct-7B (ye2025dream), LLaDA-1.5‡‡ ‡ https://huggingface.co/GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 (zhu2025llada), and LLaDA-8B-Instruct§§ § https://huggingface.co/GSAI-ML/LLaDA-8B-Instruct (zhu2025llada). This selection allows us to assess whether AXON generalizes across architectures and training recipes. In all cases, we use the publicly released checkpoints as frozen backbones. We report results on four benchmarks covering reasoning and code generation: GSM8K (cobbe2021training) and Minerva-Math (hendrycks2021measuring) for mathematical problem solving, and HumanEval (chen2021evaluating) and MBPP (austin2021program) for Python program synthesis. All methods are evaluated under identical model weights, data splits, decoding budgets, and stopping criteria, so any observed differences can be attributed to the decoding strategy rather than the evaluation protocol. Additional implementation details can be found in Appendix B.

Baselines. We compare against three recent training-free decoding strategies that cover the dominant design axes in the dLLM literature: confidence-based acceleration (wu2025fastdllm), locality-aware scheduling (LocalLeap) (kong2025localleap), and dependency-aware parallel commitment (DAWN) (luo2026dawn). LocalLeap selects anchors by confidence and commits nearby positions within a local window, while DAWN schedules parallel commitments based on inter-token dependencies. These baselines are well aligned with our setting because they are training-free and operate through explicit anchor or commitment selection, allowing AXON to be layered on top without modifying the underlying decoder.

Metrics. We report task accuracy, tokens per second (TPS), and number of function evaluations (NFE). Accuracy follows the standard evaluation protocol of each benchmark. TPS is the number of generated tokens divided by wall-clock decoding time, and NFE is the number of model forward passes required to complete generation. A desirable decoder improves accuracy or TPS while reducing NFE, or improves one metric without a comparable drop in the others.

Number of Anchors. AXON is intended to provide minimal contextual support rather than to replace the base decoder’s commit rule. We therefore evaluate a conservative default variant with a fixed budget of k=1k=1 anchor per gated intervention. We also report AXONCVR, an adaptive variant that greedily adds anchors until their coverage matches the contextual support induced by the base decoder’s proposal, i.e., until C(t)​(Sm)≥C(t)​(Sbase(t))C^{(t)}(S_{m})\geq C^{(t)}(S^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}}). See Appendix J for a study of the effect of the anchor budget.

5.2 Results

Table 1 summarizes accuracy and latency across all baselines, comparing each base decoder with the fixed-budget AXON variant and the adaptive AXONCVR variant. Across models, tasks, and decoders, AXON improves accuracy or TPS in nearly every setting while consistently reducing NFE.

Notably, several settings show simultaneous gains in accuracy and throughput. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct with LocalLeap, AXON improves HumanEval accuracy by 3.053.05 points while increasing TPS, and AXONCVR further improves throughput while remaining 2.432.43 accuracy points above the baseline. Similar trends appear on LLaDA-1.51.5. On mathematical reasoning, AXON improves both accuracy and TPS on GSM8K and Minerva-Math with LLaDA-1.51.5 and DAWN, while reducing NFE. On Dream-v0-Instruct-7B, DAWN+AXON improves GSM8K accuracy by 1.671.67 points with higher TPS, and improves both accuracy and throughput on MBPP with lower NFE. Additional per-decoder analysis is provided in Section H.

5.3 Ablations

A natural alternative to our objective (2) is additive coverage, GC⁡(S)=1|U(t)|​∑i∈U(t)∑j∈Swi​j,{\mathrm{GC}}(S)=\frac{1}{|U^{(t)}|}\sum_{i\in U^{(t)}}\sum_{j\in S}w_{ij}, which is also a submodular function. The key difference is that objective (2) (also known as facility-location) assigns credit from each uncertain position only to its best selected anchor, while additive coverage rewards all anchors which have positive weight. As a result, optimizing GC⁡(S)\mathrm{GC}(S) can repeatedly select anchors that support the same uncertain positions, whereas facility-location naturally favors diverse and non-redundant reveals through diminishing returns. Table 2 compares the two objectives. Facility-location consistently achieves lower NFE while maintaining comparable accuracy, indicating that explicitly encouraging diverse anchor coverage improves decoding efficiency. In Appendix E, We further tested whether adding an explicit redundancy penalty improves selection quality. In practice, the effect was negligible, suggesting that facility-location already discourages redundant anchors sufficiently through its saturating coverage structure. We therefore use the monotone facility-location objective throughout the paper. In addition to the anchor selection objective, the performance of AXON relies on the unified gate weight α\alpha, which balances the framework’s sensitivity between context and pace deficits. Based on our evaluations, we configure AXON with α=0.2\alpha=0.2 for the LLaDA and α=0.9\alpha=0.9 for Dream-Instruct across all main-text experiments; a comprehensive ablation of these gating dynamics and their impact on throughput and accuracy is provided in Appendix F.

6 Conclusion and Future Work

We introduced AXON, a training-free module for improving parallel decoding in diffusion language models. AXON monitors the decoding state and intervenes only when the current revealed tokens provide insufficient support to the remaining masked positions. When needed, it reveals a small set of influential and non-redundant anchors that provide targeted context for subsequent denoising steps.

Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, multiple dLLM backbones, and different decoding strategies, AXON improves the quality-latency trade-off without changing the backbone or base decoder. Our ablations show that state monitoring and coverage-based anchor selection matter, suggesting that efficient decoding should go beyond commit rules and construct useful context.

More broadly, our work sheds light on the importance of state monitoring and anchor selection in future parallel decoding, whether through gating mechanisms or self-monitoring strategies detecting when contextual support is needed.

7 Limitations

AXON improves existing parallel decoders through gated anchor interventions, but it has several limitations. First, it relies on attention and confidence signals from the frozen dLLM. These signals are lightweight and available during decoding, but they are only proxies for token influence and uncertainty. When confidence is poorly calibrated or attention does not reflect useful dependencies, anchor selection may provide limited benefit.

Second, AXON adds scoring and selection overhead. In our setting this cost is controlled because the gate fires only when needed and anchor selection is performed over a limited candidate set. For longer sequences or larger candidate pools, more approximate selection may be required.

Finally, AXON still has a quality-latency trade-off through the gate, anchor budget, and base decoder configuration. Our experiments show favorable operating points across multiple models, benchmarks, and decoder families, but the best configuration may vary by task and decoding budget. We focus on text-only reasoning and code-generation tasks; long-context, dialogue, multilingual, and multimodal settings remain future work.

References

Appendix A Additional Related Work

Adaptive and revocable commitment.

A related line changes how aggressive commitments are organized or revised over time. WINO (hong2025wino) re-masks suspicious commits to make aggressive drafts less risky, while RDD (wang2026rdd) rolls back previous blocks when the current block stalls. DCD (shu2026dcd) replaces rigid block boundaries with a confidence-aware sliding window. SlowFast (wei2025accelerating) alternates between an exploratory stage that identifies stable high-confidence spans and an accelerated stage that decodes them in parallel. Each controls the risk, consequence, or timing of a commit. AXON does not replace these mechanisms. It decides which additional reveal is worth making once the decoder’s safety rule has been applied.

Model-side and systems-level acceleration.

d3LLM (qian2026d3llm) accelerates dLLMs by retraining the model so it can expose early-decodable tokens sooner. This places d3LLM on the model-training side of the acceleration landscape, whereas AXON keeps the backbone frozen and modifies only the inference-time commit rule.

An orthogonal line reduces wall-clock cost by changing how the model is evaluated or verified, not which positions are committed. Key-value caching for dLLMs (wu2025fastdllm) avoids repeated computation across denoising steps, and speculative systems such as Spiffy (agrawal2025spiffy) accepts many drafted reveals in parallel under a lossless distribution-preserving test. This is orthogonal to the commit-selection problem we address: systems methods make individual steps cheaper, while AXON changes the commit mask when the host decoder’s own rule leaves the residual under-covered. The two compose, so we treat system acceleration as complementary to anchor selection.

Submodular optimization.

Submodular functions model diminishing returns, where the marginal gain of adding a new element decreases as the selected set grows. In our setting, once an uncertain position is already well supported by one selected anchor, adding another anchor that supports the same position should provide less additional value. This naturally motivates a facility-location objective, where each uncertain position receives credit only from its best selected anchor. Beyond our setting, submodular objectives are widely used in machine learning for selecting representative and non-redundant subsets, including data summarization chen2024guided; mualem2024submodular, active learning chen2013near, feature selection tukan2024practical, model compression el2022data, and sensor placement (zhou2022risk; tukan2023orbslam3). Greedy optimization of monotone submodular functions further admits the standard (1−1/e)(1-1/e) approximation guarantee under cardinality constraints (nemhauser1978analysis).

Appendix B Hardware and Implementation Details.

All experiments were implemented within the DAWN ¶¶ ¶ https://github.com/lizhuo-luo/DAWN diffusion decoding codebase, reusing its model weights, tokenizer settings, decoding budgets, stopping criteria, and block-sampling protocol. Throughput is measured end-to-end and includes the overhead introduced by AXON’s commit-selection step during decoding. Experiments are conducted on a cluster of 8×\timesNVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. We set βr=βu=1\beta_{r}=\beta_{u}=1 since all the involved quantities are normalized in the interval [0,1][0,1].

Appendix C Attention Dynamics and Coverage Analysis

To better understand the mechanistic impact of AXON on the diffusion decoding process, we probe the internal attention dynamics of the model during generation. Specifically, we analyze how attention patterns evolve across inference steps, how the revelation of structural anchors shifts these patterns, and how AXON accelerates the accumulation of contextual coverage. In Section C.1 evaluates LLaDA-8B Instruct on the HumanEval dataset, comparing the base decoders (Confidence, LocalLeap, and DAWN) with and without our proposed method, AXON. In Section C.2, we evaluate LLaDA-1.5 on the MBPP dataset, comparing the base DAWN decoder against DAWN equipped with AXON. Similarly, Section C.3 evaluates LLaDA-1.5 on the HumanEval dataset, comparing the base DAWN decoder against DAWN with AXON.

C.1 Qualitative Analysis of Token Dynamics

Figure 4 visualizes the step-by-step decoding trajectories to illustrate how AXON optimizes the parallel reveal mechanism compared to standard decoders. In the baseline configurations (left panels), both DAWN and Confidence decoders exhibit fragmented reveals. DAWN gets bottlenecked by local token dependencies, forcing sequential steps to resolve closely coupled syntax like _name and _check. Confidence decoding (bottom left) suffers from early global scattering, unmasking generic syntax elements (\n) prematurely without semantic coordination. In contrast, when using  AXON on top of the decoders (right panels), it intercepts these under-supported states. By injecting critical structural anchors (blue tokens like python or typing),  AXON leverages global attention paths to safely unmask entire dependent blocks simultaneously (orange tokens). This effectively resolves hard dependency cores blocks ahead of schedule, thus minimizing the total NFE required to achieve coherent code generation.

C.2 Mechanistic Impact of Anchor Commits

When AXON fires, it explicitly selects masked tokens that are highly attended to by the remaining uncertain positions. Figure 5 illustrates the immediate structural impact of revealing these anchors.

We visualize the raw 32×3232\times 32 attention slice (where rows indicate the attending position and columns indicate the attended position) just before and immediately after AXON commits its selected anchors. In the pre-commit state, attention is largely dominated by local, diagonal structures. However, in the post-commit state, distinct vertical streaks appear corresponding exactly to the positions AXON just unmasked. Once these structural anchors are converted from [MASK] to real tokens, they become highly informative landmarks. The remaining residual tokens rapidly route their attention mass to these new visible contexts, confirming that the chosen anchors successfully absorb the unresolved dependency structure of the block.

C.3 Token Unmasking Dynamics

To isolate AXON’s efficiency gains (NFE), we analyze the unmasking profiles within a single decoding block in Figure 6. Both DAWN and AXON maintain a remarkably flat per-step profile (Figure 6(b)). However, AXON consistently achieves a stable ∼\sim9% advantage at every step, resolving roughly 3.53.5 tokens compared to DAWN’s 3.23.2. As shown in the cumulative trajectory (Figure 6(a)), this minor dividend systematically compounds, allowing AXON to resolve 28/3228/32 tokens by the end of the block versus DAWN’s 26/3226/32. Aggregated over a full decoding horizon, this saves roughly 16 forward passes within the same token budget, directly explaining AXON’s lower overall NFE. The consistent gap, caused by AXON firing , confirms that submodular coverage steadily guides the model toward high-yield positions.

Proposition 1. The facility-location coverage function in Eq. 2 is monotone submodular.

Proof. Fix a denoising step tt, and let UU be the residual positions that the anchor set should support and VV be the candidate anchor positions. For any selected anchor set S⊆VS\subseteq V, recall that

C⁡(S)=∑i∈Umaxj∈S⁡wi​j,C(S)=\sum_{i\in U}\max_{j\in S}w_{ij},

with the convention that maxj∈∅⁡wi​j=0\max_{j\in\emptyset}w_{ij}=0.

Monotonicity.

Let A⊆B⊆VA\subseteq B\subseteq V. For each residual position ii,

maxj∈A⁡wi​j≤maxj∈B⁡wi​j,\max_{j\in A}w_{ij}\leq\max_{j\in B}w_{ij},

because BB contains every candidate in AA and possibly more. Summing over i∈Ui\in U gives C⁡(A)≤C⁡(B)C(A)\leq C(B). Therefore, CC is monotone.

Submodularity.

We show diminishing returns. Let A⊆B⊆VA\subseteq B\subseteq V and let e∈V∖Be\in V\setminus B. For any set S⊆VS\subseteq V, write

mi​(S)=maxj∈S⁡wi​j.m_{i}(S)=\max_{j\in S}w_{ij}.

The marginal gain from adding ee to SS is

C⁡(S∪{e})−\displaystyle C(S\cup\{e\})- C⁡(S)\displaystyle C(S)
=∑i∈U(max⁡{mi​(S),wi​e}−mi​(S))\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in U}\left(\max\{m_{i}(S),w_{ie}\}-m_{i}(S)\right)
=∑i∈Umax⁡{0,wi​e−mi​(S)}.\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in U}\max\{0,w_{ie}-m_{i}(S)\}.

Since A⊆BA\subseteq B, we have mi​(A)≤mi​(B)m_{i}(A)\leq m_{i}(B) for every i∈Ui\in U. Thus,

max⁡{0,wi​e−mi​(A)}≥max⁡{0,wi​e−mi​(B)}\max\{0,w_{ie}-m_{i}(A)\}\geq\max\{0,w_{ie}-m_{i}(B)\}

Appendix E Submodular-Objective Ablation

We ablate AXON’s set-level anchor-selection objective along two axes.

  1. 1.

    Coverage form. Facility-location (FL) CFL(t)​(S)=∑i∈Umaxj∈S⁡wi​j(t)C^{(t)}_{\mathrm{FL}}(S)=\sum_{i\in U}\max_{j\in S}w_{ij}^{(t)}, in which each uncertain position draws its coverage from the best-matching anchors within the selected set SS, versus Graph-Cut (GC) CGC(t)​(S)=∑i∈U∑j∈Swi​j(t)C^{(t)}_{\mathrm{GC}}(S)=\sum_{i\in U}\sum_{j\in S}w_{ij}^{(t)}, which instead sums each position’s affinity over all selected anchors.

  2. 2.

    Monotonicity. The monotone objective Fmono​(S)=C(t)​(S)F_{\mathrm{mono}}(S)=C^{(t)}(S) versus the non-monotone Fnonmono​(S)=C(t)​(S)−λ​R​(S)F_{\mathrm{nonmono}}(S)=C^{(t)}(S)-\lambda\,R(S), where R⁡(S)=∑{j,k}⊆Sqj​kR(S)=\sum_{\{j,k\}\subseteq S}q_{jk} is a pairwise redundancy/conflict penalty over the selected set and its weight, λ≥0\lambda\geq 0.

Protocol.

All ablation runs use the standard AXON configuration. We sweep on the two datasets. MBPP on all three models, and HumanEval on the two LLaDA models, giving five (model, task) cells. For each cell, we run both objectives in {FL\mathrm{FL}, GC\mathrm{GC}}×\times{mono, nonmono}, and for the non-monotone variants we sweep λ∈{0.2,0.3,0.4,0.5}\lambda\in\{0.2,0.3,0.4,0.5\}, giving 1010 configurations per cell.

Objective form: FL vs. GC (monotone)

We first compare the monotone facility-location (FL) objective against a graph-cut (GC). As we showed in Table 2, FL consistently outperforms GC in computational efficiency while maintaining comparable accuracy. FL achieves a lower number of function evaluations (NFE) across all five evaluation cells, yielding a lower mean NFE overall (44.89 vs. 45.95). This confirms that explicitly enforcing structural diversity prevents the model from generating additive and redundant anchor coverage, thus streamlining the generation process without sacrificing task performance.

Non-monotone penalty: λ\lambda sweep on FL

We test whether explicitly penalizing redundant anchors improves selection. As shown in Table 3, we sweep the penalty weight λ\lambda on the FL objective to observe if non-monotone regularization yields a better accuracy-NFE tradeoff compared to the purely monotone baseline (λ=0\lambda=0). The results demonstrate that introducing a non-monotone redundancy penalty provides no meaningful benefit to either task accuracy or generation efficiency. Across all five evaluation cells, shifting λ\lambda from 00 up to 0.50.5 leaves the mean accuracy virtually unchanged (fluctuating negligibly between 39.88% and 39.96%). Similarly, the computational cost remains entirely stagnant, with the mean NFE locked tightly between 44.86 and 44.91. This flat trend empirically justifies our choice of the purely monotone objective: because complex pairwise coordination penalties do not yield a superior improvement, the simpler, hyperparameter-free, monotone objective (λ=0\lambda=0) remains the optimal configuration.

Confidence Propagation From AXON

Figure 7 validates the core structural premise of AXON’s facility-location objective: anchors should be chosen not merely for their own high confidence, but for their structural capacity to propagate information to the unmasked positions that attend to them. At near-zero attention connectivity (A≈0A\approx 0), both methods perform identically, yielding a minimal confidence gain (∼0.04\sim 0.04). However, as attention weight increases, AXON’s confidence gain (Δ​confidence\Delta\text{confidence}) rises steeply and plateaus at ∼0.25​–​0.30\sim 0.25\text{--}0.30. This represents a 2x improvement over DAWN’s flat plateau (∼0.12​–​0.15\sim 0.12\text{--}0.15), proving that AXON’s submodular selection successfully routes information to highly-attending positions to accelerate model confidence.

Appendix F Gate Weight α\alpha Ablation

The hybrid gate of AXON combines two deficit signals through a single weight α\alpha: the context deficit dctx(t)d_{\text{ctx}}^{(t)} Eq. 5 and the pace deficit dpace(t)d_{\text{pace}}^{(t)} Eq. 3. It fires whenever the convex combination of their positive rectifications exceeds zero (see Eq. 6). The two endpoints recover the pure regimes: α=1\alpha\!=\!1 gates solely on the context deficit (ensuring contextual support scales with residual uncertainty and commit volume), while α=0\alpha\!=\!0 gates solely on the pace deficit (ensuring the base decoder maintains the required completion schedule).

To quantify how sensitive AXON is to this choice, we sweep α∈{0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}\alpha\in\{0,\,0.25,\,0.5,\,0.75,\,1\} on top of the DAWN base decoder (Figure 8). We evaluate four model ×\times task configurations: LLaDA-1.5 on HumanEval and MBPP, and Dream-Instruct on MBPP and GSM8K, reporting accuracy, TPS, and NFE as functions of α\alpha in Figures 8(a), 8(b), and 8(c) respectively.

Accuracy.

As illustrated in Figure 8(a), the impact of the gate weight α\alpha on generation accuracy reveals a clear, model-specific optimum, demonstrating that performance is non-monotonic. Pushing the gate to either extreme relying solely on the pace schedule (α=0\alpha=0) or exclusively on contextual support (α=1.0\alpha=1.0) is often sub-optimal, validating the need to interpolate between both deficit checks. We configure AXON with α=0.2\alpha=0.2 and α=0.9\alpha=0.9 for the LLaDA and Dream-Instruct backbones respectively across all main-text evaluations, tuning the framework to the specific failure modes of each base model.

TPS Throughput and NFE.

Generation throughput and computational overhead scale dynamically with α\alpha (see Figures 8(b) and 8(c)). By shifting the gate’s sensitivity, the framework becomes more or less tolerant of rapid, under-supported commits, thereby firing the submodular selection at different frequencies. Tuning this parameter safely accelerates generation speed and streamlines compute cost, offering a predictable trade-off trajectory against downstream quality depending on the strictness of the deployment budget.

Appendix G Relationship between confidence gain and attention

Overview and bound.

In this section we analyze how revealing a chosen anchor affects the confidence of the model at a masked position. Explicitly, we will prove an upper bound on the increase in confidence at a masked position after the anchor is revealed, in terms of the attention map AA. Let the masked position be ii, and the chosen anchor be at position ss and let ys∈𝒱∖{[MASK]}y_{s}\in\mathcal{V}\setminus\{\texttt{[MASK]}\} be the revealed (anchor) token. For simplicity, we assume that the prompt XX is empty, i.e. the input to the dLLM consists of only the response vector y(t)=(y1(t),…,yL(t))y^{(t)}=(y_{1}^{(t)},\ldots,y_{L}^{(t)}). Note that ys(t)=[MASK]y^{(t)}_{s}=\texttt{[MASK]} prior to revealing the anchor. Denote the response vector after the reveal as y~(t)\tilde{y}^{(t)}, where

y~j(t)={ysif ​j=s,yj(t)otherwise .\displaystyle\tilde{y}^{(t)}_{j}=\begin{cases}y_{s}\quad\text{if }j=s,\\ y^{(t)}_{j}\quad\text{otherwise .}\\ \end{cases}

Let 𝒱′=𝒱∖{[MASK]}\mathcal{V}^{\prime}=\mathcal{V}\setminus\{\texttt{[MASK]}\}. Thus, the increase in confidence (confidence gain) for position ii after revealing position ss can be defined as,

δi=maxv∈𝒱′⁡pθ​(yi=v|y~(t))−maxv∈𝒱′⁡pθ​(yi=v|y(t)).\displaystyle\delta_{i}=\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}^{\prime}}p_{\theta}(y_{i}=v|\tilde{y}^{(t)})-\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}^{\prime}}p_{\theta}(y_{i}=v|y^{(t)}).

While it is intuitive that the confidence of position ii should be more sensitive to the reveal of token ss when the corresponding attention entry Ai​sA_{is} is large, it is challenging to make this intuition rigorous due to the complexity of the transformer model pθp_{\theta}. To make progress in this direction, we adopt certain simplifying assumptions following prior work zhou2026attention, namely,

  1. 1.

    Following zhou2026attention, we assume that the model pθp_{\theta} is parametrized by a single layer transformer.

  2. 2.

    We assume that the attention map AA does not change after revealing position ss (similar to zhou2026attention Assumption 3.1).

Under these assumptions, we can prove that,

δi≤β​Ai​s,\displaystyle\delta_{i}\leq\beta A_{is}, (7)

for a positive constant β>0\beta>0.

Discussion of bound.

The upper bound in (7) motivates our use of attention as a measure for anchor usefulness, and the inclusion of Ai​jA_{ij} in the score wi​jw_{ij}. Indeed, (7) implies that the improvements for masked tokens (with respect to confidence) is limited by their dependency on the anchor position ss (as measured by OPENAi​s)A_{is}). This is corroborated by Figure 7, where low attention values are correlated with low confidence gains. Thus, naively choosing an anchor ss may have only a minimal effect on the confidence of remaining tokens if the column A⋅,sA_{\cdot,s} has small entries. This potentially explains the superior performance of AXON with respect to confidence gain (see Figure 7), since AXON’s submodular objective explicitly addresses this factor.

However, our analysis is limited by our assumptions. In particular, assuming a static attention map fails to account for the case where revealing an anchor ss strongly affects a masked position ii, that was earlier coupled with the anchor only through a positional dependency (e.g. adjacent tokens). For example, if the anchor is revealed to be a word that primarily occurs in a multi-token entity, e.g. “York”, the attention map can potentially change a lot for certain positions (e.g. the preceding position). Extending this analysis to consider such effects is left for future work. We now explicitly discuss the assumed architecture of pθp_{\theta}, followed by a proof of (7).

Architecture assumption.

Explicitly, let Embed:𝒱→ℝd\text{Embed}:\mathcal{V}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be a d-dimensional embedding of the token space, and Positional:{1,…,L}→ℝd\text{Positional}:\{1,\ldots,L\}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be a positional encoding function. As before, let y(t)=(y1,…,yL)y^{(t)}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{L}) be the partially masked response at diffusion step tt. Let pθ​(yi|y(t))∈ℝ|𝒱|p_{\theta}(y_{i}|y^{(t)})\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|} denote the full categorical distribution predicted by the model.

For our assumed architecture, the predicted distribution is computed in the following steps. First, the embeddings for each position ii are computed as follows,

hi=emb​(yi,i)=Embed​(yi)+Positional​(i).\displaystyle h_{i}=\text{emb}(y_{i},i)=\text{Embed}(y_{i})+\text{Positional}(i).

Given the query, key and value projection matrices WQ,WK,WVW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V}, the attention maps Ai​jA_{ij} and output representations for the attention block are computed as follows,

qi=WQ​hi,ki=WK​hi,vi=WV​hi,\displaystyle q_{i}=W_{Q}h_{i},\quad k_{i}=W_{K}h_{i},\quad v_{i}=W_{V}h_{i},
Ai​j=exp​(qi⊤​kj/d)∑jexp​(qi⊤​kj/d),\displaystyle A_{ij}=\frac{\text{exp}(q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}/\sqrt{d})}{\sum_{j}\text{exp}(q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}/\sqrt{d})},

Finally, a fully connected layer (with parameters (W,b)(W,b)), followed by a softmax activation, is applied to each position independently to obtain the predicted distributions as follows :

pθ​(yi|y(t))=Softmax​(W​zi+b).\displaystyle p_{\theta}(y_{i}|y^{(t)})=\text{Softmax}(Wz_{i}+b).

Define the notation,

g​(z)=Softmax​(W​z+b).\displaystyle g(z)=\text{Softmax}(Wz+b).

Since gg is differentiable everywhere, therefore gg is also locally Lipschitz continuous. Appendix H Effects Of AXON On The Decoders

The interaction between anchor selection and accelerated decoding strategies is heavily dependent on the structural representation mechanism of the method. For the simple thresholding-based methods, which make decisions to immediately commit a token only based on a flat probability threshold, AXON acts as a co-dependency filter; by evaluating global information entropy, it penalizes mutual context redundancy, eliminating simultaneous-masking conflicts and yielding a steady recovery in both generation quality and Throughput. For heuristically-driven spatial methods (LocalLeap), which expand unmasking zones natively by lowering confidence thresholds uniformly within a fixed, linear geometric radius around predicted anchors, AXON enforces a diversity constraint that eliminates anchor clumping, preventing localized text degradation and primarily optimizing Accuracy. For graph-driven structural methods (DAWN), which is based on model token interdependencies by extracting raw attention maps and utilizing a Maximum Independent Set solver to parallelize non-conflicting tokens, AXON provides global informational pillars that clarify noisy attention maps, allowing the dependency solver to uncover massive parallel sets and maximize throughput (TPS).

Appendix I Analysis of Gate Firing Patterns

Figure 9 visualizes the probability of the AXON gate firing (G(t)=1\mathrm{G}^{(t)}=1).

Across blocks (Macro).

Figure 9a shows that activations are heavily front-loaded. Early in the generation, causal context is sparse and residual uncertainty is high, requiring AXON to intervene frequently. As the sequence progresses and reliable context accumulates, the gate naturally backs off.

Within blocks (Micro).

Figure 9b reveals that interventions concentrate almost entirely at Step 0. When a new block opens, structural support is minimal. AXON immediately injects high-leverage anchors to clear this bottleneck, allowing the base decoder to rapidly resolve the rest of the block uninterrupted. The truncated right edge of the heatmap visually confirms that this early intervention reduces the total steps required to finish the block.

Appendix J Effect of the Number of Anchors

AXON uses a small anchor budget because the goal is not to maximize the number of additional committed tokens, but to reveal a small number of tokens that provide high contextual support to uncertain residual positions. The default variant uses a fixed budget of k=1k=1 anchor whenever the gate fires. This setting keeps the intervention cheap and conservative, while the facility-location objective discourages redundant reveals by giving each uncertain position credit only for its best selected anchor.

We also evaluate AXONCVR, an adaptive coverage-matching variant. Let

τ(t)=C(t)​(Sbase(t))\tau^{(t)}=C^{(t)}\!\left(S^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}}\right)

denote the contextual coverage induced by the base decoder’s proposal. Starting from S0=∅S_{0}=\varnothing, AXONCVR greedily adds the candidate anchor with largest marginal gain under C(t)C^{(t)} until

C(t)​(Sm)≥τ(t).C^{(t)}(S_{m})\geq\tau^{(t)}.

Equivalently, its final cardinality is

|SCVR⋆(t)|=min⁡{m≥1:C(t)​(Sm)≥τ(t)}.|S^{\star(t)}_{\mathrm{CVR}}|=\min\left\{m\geq 1:\ C^{(t)}(S_{m})\geq\tau^{(t)}\right\}.

This gives the adaptive variant a per-step scale for how much contextual support is needed, while still selecting anchors according to the same non-redundant coverage objective. For any realized cardinality mm, the greedy prefix retains the standard (1−1/e)(1-1/e) approximation guarantee for monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality budget of mm.

In Figure 10, we ablate the fixed per-fire anchor budget and report its effect on NFE, tokens per second, and accuracy.

Larger budgets commit more tokens per intervention, shrinking the residual mask M(t)M^{(t)} and lowering NFE monotonically. Throughput tracks NFE initially but plateaus once the greedy submodular search overhead begins to dominate the savings. Accuracy follows an inverted U-shape: a small set of high-confidence anchors absorbs the attention of uncertain residuals and resolves stalled positions, while larger budgets force selection from the low-confidence tail of the candidate pool V(t)V^{(t)}, injecting noise that propagates through subsequent denoising steps. The settings deployed in Section 5 sit at the Pareto frontier of this trade-off.

Appendix K Context Deficit Normalization β\beta

The context deficit dctx(t)d_{\text{ctx}}^{(t)} (Eq. 5) evaluates the contextual support g(t)g^{(t)} against two distinct signals: the decoding pace r(t)r^{(t)} and the residual uncertainty uM(t)u_{M}^{(t)}. While all three quantities naturally fall within the [0,1][0,1] interval, they originate from different distributions and lack a universally scaled theoretical equivalence. As discussed in Appendix G, this correlates between attention mass and uncertainty reduction. However, to account for potential distribution shifts across different model architectures, one could introduce scaling coefficients βr,βu>0\beta_{r},\beta_{u}>0 to explicitly calibrate these thresholds:

dctx(t)=max⁡(βr​r(t),βu​uM(t))−g(t).d_{\text{ctx}}^{(t)}=\max\!\big(\beta_{r}r^{(t)},\,\beta_{u}u_{M}^{(t)}\big)-g^{(t)}. (9)

Setting βr=βu=1\beta_{r}=\beta_{u}=1 establishes a parameter-free uniform-prior baseline which we use in our experiments in Table 1. To evaluate the sensitivity of AXON to these normalization constants, we perform a 2D grid search over βr,βu∈{0.2,0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0}\beta_{r},\beta_{u}\in\{0.2,0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0\} (Figure 11), reporting Accuracy, TPS, and NFE.

Accuracy.

In Figure 11(a), the grid search reveals a clear trade-off spectrum depending on the strictness of the gate. At lower threshold values (β≤0.5\beta\leq 0.5), the gate is overly permissive; it frequently fails to intervene when the base decoder lacks sufficient structural context, causing generation accuracy to drop. As the β\beta coefficients increase, the gate becomes stricter, forcing the model to rely more heavily on the injected anchors which pushes accuracy.

TPS Throughput and NFE.

While aggressive gating (high β\beta) yields marginal accuracy gains, it incurs a catastrophic penalty to efficiency. Thresholds above 1.01.0 force the gate to fire almost continuously which inflates the number of forward passes (NFE) and decreasing throughput (TPS), as depicted in Figures 11(c) and 11(b) respectively, but with a direct trade-off with accuracy.
